  3. (C) 6 ∣ 12 and no element of P lies strictly between 6 and 12 (the divisors of 12 above 6 are only 12). TRUE.
  4. (D) 6 ∣ 24, but 12 ∈ P satisfies 6 ∣ 12 ∣ 24, so 12 lies strictly between them. FALSE.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Divisibility is taken as covering. Covering is a statement about the *specific* poset: 24 covers 8 here precisely because 12 is not a multiple of 8, while 24 fails to cover 6 because 12 is a multiple of 6.

DM-REL2-Q10MCQeasy

In the divisibility poset on P = {1, 2, 4, 8}, which element does 4 cover?

  1. 1
  2. 2
  3. 8
  4. 4 covers no element of P.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. b covers a when a ∣ b, a ≠ b, and no third element of the poset lies strictly between them.

Step by step.

  1. The elements of P dividing 4 are 1 and 2.
  2. Since 1 ∣ 2 ∣ 4, the element 1 lies strictly below 4 through 2, so 4 does not cover 1.
  3. Nothing in P lies strictly between 2 and 4, so 4 covers 2.
  4. Answer: 4 covers 2.

Answer: Option (B) — 2

Common misconception. Reading "covers" as "is divisible by", which would make 4 cover both 1 and 2.

DM-REL2-Q11MCQmedium

In the divisibility poset on {1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30}, how many edges does the Hasse diagram have?

  1. 10
  2. 11
  3. 12
  4. 14
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Hasse-diagram edges are the covering relations; in a divisor-closed set, b covers a exactly when b/a is prime.

Step by step.

  1. Group by the number of prime factors: 1 at level 0; 2, 3, 5 at level 1; 6, 10, 15 at level 2; 30 at level 3.
  2. Level 0 to level 1: 2, 3, 5 covers 1 — three edges.
  3. Level 1 to level 2: 6 covers 2 and 3; 10 covers 2 and 5; 15 covers 3 and 5 — six edges.
  4. Level 2 to level 3: 30 covers 6, 10 and 15 — three edges.
  5. Total 3 + 6 + 3 = 12.

Answer: Option (C) — 12

Common misconception. Drawing an edge for every divisibility pair. That draws the whole relation, not its transitive reduction.

DM-REL2-Q12NATmedium

In the divisibility poset on P = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12, 18, 36}, how many edges does the Hasse diagram have?
(Enter an integer.)

Answer: 10

Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The set is closed under divisors, so b covers a exactly when b/a is prime.

Step by step.

  1. Covers of 1: 2 and 3 (both quotients prime) — 2 edges.
  2. Covers of 2 and 3: 4 covers 2; 6 covers 2 and 3 — 3 edges.
  3. Covers of 4 and 6: 12 covers 4 and 6; 18 covers 6 only, because 18/6 = 3 and nothing in P lies between 6 and 18 — 3 edges.
  4. Covers of 12 and 18: 36 covers both — 2 edges.
  5. Total 2 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 10.

Answer: 10

Common misconception. Adding edges such as 1 to 4, 1 to 6 or 6 to 36. None is a cover: 4/1 = 4 is composite, and 12 lies strictly between 6 and 36.

DM-REL2-Q13MSQhard

Consider the divisibility poset on P = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36}. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. 36 is the greatest element of P.
  2. The pair {12, 18} has no least upper bound in P.
  3. The least upper bound of {4, 6} in P is 12.
  4. The element 6 covers exactly two elements of P.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. In a divisor-closed poset the join is the lcm and the meet is the gcd; the only way a join can fail is if the lcm leaves the set.

Step by step.

  1. 36 is divisible by every element of P, so it is the greatest element. (A) is TRUE.
  2. Upper bounds of {12, 18} in P are the multiples of lcm(12,18) = 36 that lie in P: only 36. So the lub exists and equals 36. (B) is FALSE.
  3. Upper bounds of {4, 6} are 12 and 36; the least is 12. (C) is TRUE.
  4. 6/2 = 3 and 6/3 = 2 are prime while 6/1 = 6 is not, so 6 covers exactly 2 and 3. (D) is TRUE.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D)

Common misconception. Expecting the lub to be a small, "nearby" element. When a pair is spread across two branches, the lub is often the top element.

Lattices in posets 8
DM-REL1-Q10MCQeasy

Which of the following posets is NOT a lattice?

  1. (𝒫(S), ⊆) for a set S
  2. (ℤ⁺, ∣) — the positive integers under divisibility
  3. The poset with elements {0, a, b} where 0 < a, 0 < b and a, b are incomparable
  4. ({1, 2, 3, 6, 12}, ∣)
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A lattice is a poset in which every pair of elements has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound inside the poset.

Step by step.

  1. (A): A ∨ B = A ∪ B and A ∧ B = A ∩ B — always a lattice.
  2. (B): a ∨ b = lcm(a,b) and a ∧ b = gcd(a,b) — always a lattice.
  3. (C): the upper bounds of a and b form the empty set, so no least upper bound exists. Not a lattice.
  4. (D): the set is divisor-closed, so every pair has both a join and a meet inside it: 2 ∨ 3 = lcm(2,3) = 6, 6 ∨ 12 = 12, 2 ∧ 12 = gcd(2,12) = 2, 3 ∧ 12 = 3. A lattice.

Answer: Option (C) — the three-element V-poset.

Common misconception. "Incomparable" is confused with "no join". Two incomparable elements can still have a join — the failure in (C) is that they have no common upper bound at all.

DM-REL1-Q11MCQmedium

For a positive integer n, let D(n) be the lattice of positive divisors of n under divisibility. D(n) is a Boolean lattice exactly when

  1. n is prime
  2. n is a product of distinct primes
  3. n is a power of a prime
  4. n is even
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. If n = p₁^{e₁} … p_k^{e_k}, then D(n) is isomorphic to the product of chains C_{e₁+1} × … × C_{e_k+1}. A Boolean lattice is a product of copies of the two-element chain.

Step by step.

  1. Each divisor corresponds to a tuple of exponents (a₁, …, a_k) with 0 ≤ aᵢ ≤ eᵢ, ordered coordinatewise.
  2. That is a product of chains of lengths eᵢ + 1.
  3. A product of chains is Boolean only when every factor is the two-element chain, i.e. every eᵢ = 1.
  4. So D(n) ≅ 2^k exactly when n is squarefree, a product of distinct primes.

Answer: Option (B) — n is a product of distinct primes.

Common misconception. Prime powers feel "simple" and are assumed to give Boolean lattices; in fact they give chains, the opposite extreme.

DM-REL1-Q19MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about lattices are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Every finite lattice has a least element and a greatest element.
  2. In a distributive lattice an element has at most one complement.
  3. Every lattice is distributive.
  4. In every bounded lattice every element has a complement.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A finite lattice is bounded because the join and meet of all elements exist; distributivity is an extra axiom, and complementedness is another.

Step by step.

  1. (A): in a finite lattice the join of all elements is the greatest element and the meet of all elements is the least element. TRUE.
  2. (B): if b and c are both complements of a, then b = b ∧ 1 = b ∧ (a ∨ c) = (b ∧ a) ∨ (b ∧ c) = 0 ∨ (b ∧ c) = b ∧ c, and symmetrically c = b ∧ c, so b = c. TRUE.
  3. (C): the diamond M₃ and the pentagon N₅ are lattices that are not distributive. FALSE.
  4. (D): in N₅ the middle element has no complement. FALSE.

Answer: Options (A) and (B).

Common misconception. Bounded is read as complemented. A bounded lattice may have elements with no complement at all, and in a non-distributive lattice an element may have several.

DM-REL1-Q23NAThard

In the divisor lattice D(72) — the positive divisors of 72 ordered by divisibility — how many elements have a complement?
(Enter an integer.)

Answer: 4

Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. In a bounded lattice, e is a complement of d when d ∧ e = 1 and d ∨ e = 72, i.e. gcd(d,e) = 1 and lcm(d,e) = 72.

Step by step.

  1. Write 72 = 2³ · 3². A divisor is d = 2^i 3^j with 0 ≤ i ≤ 3, 0 ≤ j ≤ 2.
  2. The two conditions together force d · e = 72, so e = 72/d is the only candidate.
  3. Then gcd(d, 72/d) = 1 requires d to take each prime's full exponent or none: i ∈ {0, 3} and j ∈ {0, 2}.
  4. That gives 2 × 2 = 4 divisors: 1, 8, 9, 72, with complements 72, 9, 8, 1.

Answer: 4

Common misconception. D(72) is distributive and bounded, so students assume every element has a complement. Distributive + bounded is not complemented — the standard counterexample is exactly this kind of divisor lattice.

DM-REL2-Q14MCQeasy

In the divisor lattice D(12) = ({1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12}, ∣), what is the join (least upper bound) of 4 and 6?

  1. 2
  2. 12
  3. 24
  4. 4 and 6 have no join in D(12).
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. In a divisor lattice the join is the least common multiple, provided it belongs to the lattice; the meet is the greatest common divisor.

Step by step.

  1. Common upper bounds of 4 and 6 are the common multiples: 12, 24, 36, …
  2. Among those, only 12 belongs to D(12).
  3. So the least upper bound is 12.
  4. Answer: 12.

Answer: Option (B) — 12

Common misconception. Swapping join and meet. The lcm is the join (an upper bound); the gcd is the meet.

DM-REL2-Q15MCQmedium

For which of the following values of n is the divisor lattice D(n) NOT a Boolean lattice?

  1. n = 6
  2. n = 30
  3. n = 12
  4. n = 210
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. D(n) is a Boolean lattice exactly when n is squarefree, that is, a product of distinct primes.

Step by step.

  1. If n = p₁p₂…p_k with the primes p_i distinct, then each divisor corresponds to a choice of exponents 0 ≤ e_i ≤ 1 and D(n) is isomorphic to the subset lattice of a k-element set.
  2. 6 = 2·3, 30 = 2·3·5 and 210 = 2·3·5·7 are all squarefree, so their divisor lattices are Boolean, on 2, 3 and 4 atoms respectively.
  3. 12 = 2²·3 is not squarefree, and D(12) has 6 elements — no Boolean lattice has 6 elements.
  4. Answer: n = 12.

Answer: Option (C) — n = 12

Common misconception. Judging by size or by "highly composite". The test is squarefreeness of n, not how many divisors it has.

DM-REL2-Q16NAThard

In the divisor lattice D(36), how many elements have a complement?
(Enter an integer.)

Answer: 4

Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. An element x has a complement y when x ∨ y = 1̂ and x ∧ y = 0̂. Since 36 = 2²·3², the lattice is the product of two 3-element chains of exponents.

Step by step.

  1. Since 36 = 2²·3², the lattice is D(36) ≅ C₃ × C₃, a product of two copies of the exponent chain C₃ = {0, 1, 2}.
  2. An element (a,b) has complement (c,d) exactly when a ∨ c = 2, a ∧ c = 0, b ∨ d = 2 and b ∧ d = 0.
  3. Inside C₃ only 0 and 2 have complements: for a = 1, 1 ∨ c = 2 forces c = 2, but then 1 ∧ 2 = 1 ≠ 0.
  4. So each coordinate must be 0 or 2, giving 2 × 2 = 4 elements: 1, 4, 9 and 36.
  5. Check: the complement pairs are (1, 36) and (4, 9).

Answer: 4

Common misconception. Assuming every element of a bounded lattice has a complement. Here 6 is the counterexample: no y satisfies both gcd(6,y) = 1 and lcm(6,y) = 36.

DM-REL2-Q17MSQmedium

In a lattice (L, ≤) with join ∨ and meet ∧, which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. a ∧ (a ∨ b) = a for all a, b ∈ L.
  2. a ∨ (a ∧ b) = b for all a, b ∈ L.
  3. If a ≤ b then a ∧ b = a.
  4. Every bounded lattice is complemented.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The join is the least upper bound and the meet the greatest lower bound; the absorption laws follow directly from those two definitions.

Step by step.

  1. (A) Since a ≤ a ∨ b, the element a ∨ b is an upper bound of both a and a ∨ b, so a ∧ (a ∨ b) = a. TRUE.
  2. (B) Take b < a. Then a ∨ (a ∧ b) = a ∨ b = a, and the claim would give a = b. FALSE.
  3. (C) If a ≤ b then a is a lower bound of both and no larger element is, so a ∧ b = a. TRUE.
  4. (D) Take the five-element lattice 0 < a, b < 1, where a, b are incomparable. It is bounded, but a has no complement: no element both meets it at 0 and joins with it to 1. FALSE.

Answer: Options (A) and (C)

Common misconception. Treating absorption as if the two variables swapped places. Both laws return the repeated variable, not the other one.

Composition & transitive closure 8
DM-REL1-Q12MCQeasy

Let R = {(1,2), (2,3)} on A = {1, 2, 3}. What is the composite relation R ∘ R?

  1. {(1,2), (2,3)}
  2. {(1,3)}
  3. {(1,2), (2,3), (1,3)}
  4. ∅
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. (a,c) ∈ S ∘ R exactly when some b satisfies (a,b) ∈ R and (b,c) ∈ S — a two-step walk.

Step by step.

  1. Start at 1: the only pair out of 1 is (1,2), so continue from 2. The only pair out of 2 is (2,3), giving (1,3).
  2. Start at 2: leads to 3, and nothing leaves 3, so no pair.
  3. Start at 3: nothing leaves 3, so no pair.
  4. Hence R ∘ R = {(1,3)}.

Answer: Option (B) — {(1,3)}.

Common misconception. R² is read as "the transitive closure" or as "square each element". Composition is path concatenation of exactly two steps.

DM-REL1-Q13MCQmedium

Let R = {(1,2), (2,1), (3,4)} on A = {1, 2, 3, 4}. How many ordered pairs are in the transitive closure R⁺?

  1. 4
  2. 5
  3. 6
  4. 7
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The transitive closure contains (a,b) exactly when a walk of positive length runs from a to b.

Step by step.

  1. The pairs (1,2) and (2,1) form a 2-cycle, so from 1 you can reach 2, and from 2 you can reach 1.
  2. Composing the cycle with itself gives (1,1) and (2,2), which must be added.
  3. The pair (3,4) is isolated: nothing leaves 4 and nothing enters 3, so it generates no new pair.
  4. So R⁺ = {(1,2), (2,1), (1,1), (2,2), (3,4)} — five pairs.

Answer: Option (B) — 5 ordered pairs.

Common misconception. The transitive closure is assumed to be the reflexive-transitive closure. Here the diagonal pairs come from the cycle, not from reflexivity — (3,3) and (4,4) are correctly absent.

DM-REL1-Q20MSQeasy

Let R and S be relations on a set A. Which of the following identities hold? (Select all that apply.)

  1. (R ∪ S)⁻¹ = R⁻¹ ∪ S⁻¹
  2. (R ∩ S)⁻¹ = R⁻¹ ∩ S⁻¹
  3. (S ∘ R)⁻¹ = R⁻¹ ∘ S⁻¹
  4. R ∘ R⁻¹ is the identity relation on A
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Inversion commutes with union, intersection and difference because it only swaps the two coordinates of each pair; composition reverses the order of the factors.

Step by step.

  1. (A): (a,b) ∈ (R ∪ S)⁻¹ ⇔ (b,a) ∈ R ∪ S ⇔ (b,a) ∈ R or (b,a) ∈ S ⇔ (a,b) ∈ R⁻¹ ∪ S⁻¹. TRUE.
  2. (B): the same argument with "or" replaced by "and". TRUE.
  3. (C): (a,c) ∈ (S ∘ R)⁻¹ ⇔ (c,a) ∈ S ∘ R ⇔ ∃b, (c,b) ∈ S, (b,a) ∈ R ⇔ ∃b, (b,c) ∈ S⁻¹, (a,b) ∈ R⁻¹ ⇔ (a,c) ∈ R⁻¹ ∘ S⁻¹. TRUE.
  4. (D): R ∘ R⁻¹ = {(a,a) : ∃b, (a,b) ∈ R}. If some element of A has no R-image, its diagonal pair is missing, so the relation is only a subset of I_A. FALSE.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. The inverse of a composite is written in the same order. It must be reversed: (S ∘ R)⁻¹ = R⁻¹ ∘ S⁻¹, like inverting a product of matrices.

DM-REL1-Q25NATmedium

On A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} let R = {(1,2), (2,3), (3,1), (4,5)}. How many ordered pairs are in the transitive closure R⁺?
(Enter an integer.)

Answer: 10

Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The transitive closure contains (a,b) exactly when a walk of positive length runs from a to b.

Step by step.

  1. Elements 1, 2, 3 form a directed cycle 1 → 2 → 3 → 1, so every element of the cycle reaches every element of the cycle.
  2. That contributes 3² = 9 pairs.
  3. The pair (4,5) is isolated from the cycle and adds exactly one pair.
  4. Total: 9 + 1 = 10.

Answer: 10

Common misconception. Students count only the cycle's own three pairs plus (4,5) and get 4, forgetting that a strongly connected component contributes all s² pairs.

DM-REL2-Q18MCQeasy

Let R = {(1,2), (2,3)} and S = {(2,3), (3,1)} on A = {1, 2, 3}. Which of the following equals S ∘ R?

  1. {(1,3), (2,1)}
  2. {(1,3), (1,1)}
  3. {(2,3), (3,1)}
  4. ∅
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. S ∘ R consists of the pairs (x,z) for which some y satisfies (x,y) ∈ R and (y,z) ∈ S — that is, of all two-step walks, with the intermediate vertex suppressed.

Step by step.

  1. (1,2) ∈ R and (2,3) ∈ S give (1,3).
  2. (2,3) ∈ R and (3,1) ∈ S give (2,1).
  3. No other pair of R can be followed by a pair of S, so the composition is exactly {(1,3), (2,1)}.
  4. Answer: S ∘ R = {(1,3), (2,1)}.

Answer: Option (A)

Common misconception. Reading S ∘ R right to left as "apply S then R". In S ∘ R the right-hand factor R acts first.

DM-REL2-Q19MCQmedium

Let R and S be relations on a set A. Which of the following statements is TRUE in general?

  1. R ∘ S = S ∘ R for all relations R and S.
  2. If R and S are both transitive, then R ∪ S is transitive.
  3. If R and S are both reflexive, then R ∘ S is reflexive.
  4. If R and S are both symmetric, then R ∘ S is symmetric.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Composition preserves reflexivity but not symmetry, and it does not commute; unions preserve neither transitivity nor anything else for free.

Step by step.

  1. (C) If R and S are reflexive then for every a ∈ A both (a,a) ∈ R and (a,a) ∈ S lie in the respective relations, so (a,a) ∈ R ∘ S. TRUE.
  2. (A) fails on A = {1, 2, 3} with R = {(1,2)} and S = {(2,3)}: then S ∘ R = {(1,3)} while R ∘ S = ∅.
  3. (B) fails for the same pair: both relations are transitive, yet R ∪ S = {(1,2), (2,3)} misses (1,3).
  4. (D) fails with R = {(1,2), (2,1)} and S = {(2,3), (3,2)}: then S ∘ R = {(1,3)}, which is not symmetric.

Answer: Option (C)

Common misconception. Believing that any property shared by two relations is inherited by their union or composition. Only some properties are preserved, and by some operations.

DM-REL2-Q20NATeasy

On A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} let R = {(1,2), (2,3), (1,3), (3,4), (4,5), (2,5)}. How many ordered pairs must be added to R to obtain its transitive closure?
(Enter an integer.)

Answer: 4

Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The transitive closure is the reachability relation of the digraph of R: (x,y) lies in R⁺ exactly when a directed path of positive length runs from x to y.

Step by step.

  1. Reachability: 1 reaches 2, 3, 4, 5; 2 reaches 3, 4, 5; 3 reaches 4, 5; 4 reaches 5; 5 reaches nothing.
  2. So R⁺ = {(1,2), (1,3), (1,4), (1,5), (2,3), (2,4), (2,5), (3,4), (3,5), (4,5)}.
  3. R contains 6 pairs and R⁺ contains 10.
  4. The pairs to add are (1,4), (1,5), (2,4), (3,5) — four of them.

Answer: 4

Common misconception. Stopping after one round of composition, which adds only (1,4) and (2,4) and misses the paths of length 3 and 4.

DM-REL2-Q25MCQeasy

Let R = {(1,2), (2,3), (3,1)} on A = {1, 2, 3}. Which of the following equals R ∘ R?

  1. {(1,3), (2,1), (3,2)}
  2. {(1,2), (2,3), (3,1)}
  3. {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3)}
  4. ∅
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. R ∘ R advances every walk by one step: (x,z) lies in R ∘ R exactly when a path of length two runs from x to z.

Step by step.

  1. (1,2) then (2,3) gives (1,3).
  2. (2,3) then (3,1) gives (2,1).
  3. (3,1) then (1,2) gives (3,2).
  4. So R ∘ R = {(1,3), (2,1), (3,2)}.

Answer: Option (A)

Common misconception. Assuming %s whenever %s is a cycle. Composition shifts the cycle by one step instead of returning it.

Counting relations 8
DM-REL1-Q14MCQeasy

How many relations are there on a set with three elements?

  1. 64
  2. 256
  3. 512
  4. 729
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A relation on A is any subset of A × A, so the count is 2^{|A|²}.

Step by step.

  1. With |A| = 3, the product set has 3 × 3 = 9 ordered pairs.
  2. Each of those nine pairs is independently either in or out of the relation.
  3. So the number of relations is 2⁹ = 512.

Answer: Option (C) — 512.

Common misconception. The exponent is |A × A| = n², not n. Students who write 2³ = 8 are counting subsets of A instead.

DM-REL1-Q15MCQmedium

How many reflexive relations are there on a set with four elements?

  1. 1024
  2. 2048
  3. 4096
  4. 65536
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Reflexivity forces the n diagonal pairs into the relation; every other pair stays free, so the count is 2^{n² − n}.

Step by step.

  1. There are 4² = 16 ordered pairs in total.
  2. The four diagonal pairs (a,a) must be included — no freedom there.
  3. The remaining 16 − 4 = 12 pairs are free.
  4. So the number of reflexive relations is 2¹² = 4096.

Answer: Option (C) — 4096.

Common misconception. Students subtract n from n² but then compute 2^n instead of 2^{n²−n}; or they forget that the diagonal is forced *in*, not just removed from the count.

DM-REL1-Q21NATeasy

How many symmetric relations are there on a set with three elements?
(Enter an integer.)

Answer: 64

Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A symmetric relation is determined independently on the diagonal pairs and on each unordered pair {a, b}: for off-diagonal pairs symmetry forces both (a,b) and (b,a) to be in, or both to be out.

Step by step.

  1. There are 3 diagonal pairs, each free: 2³ choices.
  2. There are C(3,2) = 3 unordered off-diagonal pairs; symmetry makes each an all-or-nothing choice: 2³ choices.
  3. Multiply: 2³ · 2³ = 2⁶ = 64.

Answer: 64

Common misconception. Counting 2⁹ = 512 by treating all nine pairs as independent — symmetry couples the pairs (a,b) and (b,a).

DM-REL1-Q22NATmedium

How many antisymmetric relations are there on a set with two elements?
(Enter an integer.)

Answer: 12

Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Antisymmetry only constrains pairs of the form (a,b) and (b,a) with a ≠ b: they may not both be present.

Step by step.

  1. Let A = {1, 2}. The two diagonal pairs are unconstrained: 2² = 4 choices.
  2. For the pair {1, 2} there are three legal states: include neither, include only (1,2), include only (2,1).
  3. Multiply: 4 × 3 = 12.

Answer: 12

Common misconception. Counting 2⁴ = 16 by treating all four pairs as free — the state "both (1,2) and (2,1)" is exactly what antisymmetry forbids.

DM-REL2-Q21MCQeasy

How many irreflexive relations are there on a set with three elements?

  1. 8
  2. 64
  3. 512
  4. 729
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A relation on a set of n elements is a subset of A × A, which has n² pairs; each property fixes or frees some of those pairs.

Step by step.

  1. For n = 3, the set A × A has 9 ordered pairs.
  2. Irreflexive means the three diagonal pairs (a,a) are all excluded.
  3. The remaining 6 off-diagonal pairs are unconstrained, and each may be in or out.
  4. So the count is 2⁶ = 64.

Answer: Option (B) — 64

Common misconception. Using 2^(n²) for every property. Each constraint removes free pairs and shrinks the exponent.

DM-REL2-Q22MCQmedium

How many relations on a set with four elements are both reflexive and antisymmetric?

  1. 64
  2. 216
  3. 729
  4. 4096
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Reflexivity fixes the diagonal pairs; antisymmetry constrains each unordered off-diagonal pair to at most one direction.

Step by step.

  1. Reflexivity forces all 4 diagonal pairs to be present — 1 way.
  2. The 12 off-diagonal pairs fall into 6 unordered pairs {a, b}.
  3. For each unordered pair, antisymmetry permits exactly three states: neither directed pair, only (a,b), or only (b,a).
  4. Total 3⁶ = 729.

Answer: Option (C) — 729

Common misconception. Giving each unordered pair two choices. Antisymmetry leaves three, because either direction may be present or neither.

DM-REL2-Q23MCQhard

How many partial orders are there on a set with three elements?

  1. 12
  2. 19
  3. 27
  4. 33
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A partial order is a reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive relation; on three labelled elements it is best counted by the shape of its Hasse diagram.

Step by step.

  1. Antichain (no comparabilities): 1 order.
  2. Exactly one comparable pair: choose the two elements and the direction, 3 · 2 = 6.
  3. A chain of three: 3! = 6 linear orders.
  4. A V shape: one minimal element below two incomparable elements — choose the minimum, 3 orders.
  5. A Λ shape: one maximal element above two incomparable elements — choose the maximum, 3 orders.
  6. Total 1 + 6 + 6 + 3 + 3 = 19.

Answer: Option (B) — 19

Common misconception. Counting reflexive antisymmetric relations and assuming transitivity is automatic. It is not: {(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2),(2,3)} is reflexive and antisymmetric but not transitive.

DM-REL2-Q24MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about counting relations on a set A with |A| = n are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Every relation on A is a subset of A × A, and every subset of A × A is a relation on A.
  2. The number of symmetric relations on A is 2^(n(n+1)/2).
  3. The number of antisymmetric relations on A is 2^(n(n−1)/2).
  4. A reflexive relation on A contains exactly n² − n ordered pairs.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Relations on A correspond exactly to subsets of A × A, so counting relations means counting free choices over the pairs of A × A.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is the definition; the correspondence is a bijection. TRUE.
  2. (B) A symmetric relation is free on the n diagonal pairs and on the n(n−1)/2 unordered off-diagonal pairs, so 2^(n + n(n−1)/2) = 2^(n(n+1)/2). TRUE.
  3. (C) fails: antisymmetry allows three states per unordered off-diagonal pair, giving 2ⁿ · 3^(n(n−1)/2).
  4. (D) fails: reflexivity forces at least the n diagonal pairs and says nothing about the off-diagonal ones, so any number from n up to n² is possible.

Answer: Options (A) and (B)

Common misconception. Assuming symmetric and antisymmetric relations are counted by the same expression. The antisymmetric count carries an extra factor 2ⁿ.

Unit 5 — Functions 50 solved questions
Injective / surjective / bijective 10
DM-FUN1-Q01MCQeasy

Let f : ℤ → ℤ be defined by f(x) = 2x. Which one of the following describes f correctly?

  1. f is bijective.
  2. f is injective but not surjective.
  3. f is surjective but not injective.
  4. f is neither injective nor surjective.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Injectivity asks whether two different inputs can share an output; surjectivity asks whether every element of the codomain is hit at all. On infinite domains the two are independent.

Step by step.

  1. Suppose f(a) = f(b), i.e. 2a = 2b. Dividing by 2 gives a = b, so f is injective.
  2. Now take the codomain element 3. If 2x = 3 then x = 3/2, which is not an integer, so 3 has no preimage in ℤ.
  3. More generally only even integers are values of f, so the image is 2ℤ ⊊ ℤ.
  4. Hence f is injective and not surjective.

Answer: Option (B) — injective, not surjective.

Common misconception. Students transfer the finite-set rule "injective ⇔ surjective" to ℤ. That equivalence needs the domain and codomain to be finite of equal size; on infinite sets x ↦ 2x is injective but leaves half the codomain untouched.

DM-FUN1-Q02MCQmedium

Let ℤ⁺ = {1, 2, 3, …}. Which one of the following functions f : ℤ⁺ → ℤ⁺ is surjective (onto)?

  1. f(n) = n + 1
  2. f(n) = 2n
  3. f(n) = ⌈n/2⌉
  4. f(n) = n²
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A function into ℤ⁺ is surjective when every positive integer occurs as a value. For a candidate, the quickest test is to try to hit a small target such as 1.

Step by step.

  1. (A) n + 1 ≥ 2 for every n ≥ 1, so 1 is never attained. Not surjective.
  2. (B) 2n is even, so 1 (and every odd number) is missed. Not surjective.
  3. (C) ⌈n/2⌉ takes the values 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, … for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, …. Every k ∈ ℤ⁺ is attained, for instance at n = 2k − 1. Surjective.
  4. (D) n² attains only perfect squares, so 2 is missed. Not surjective.

Answer: Option (C) — f(n) = ⌈n/2⌉.

Common misconception. Assuming a "spreading out" function such as 2n covers everything because it grows. Growth is irrelevant to surjectivity; what matters is which values are hit.

DM-FUN1-Q03MSQeasy

Let A and B be finite sets with |A| = |B| = n ≥ 1, and let f : A → B. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. If f is injective, then f is bijective.
  2. If f is surjective, then f is bijective.
  3. Every function f : A → B is bijective.
  4. If f is bijective, then f has an inverse function f⁻¹ : B → A.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. For a function between finite sets of equal size, injective, surjective and bijective are the same condition. That is the pigeonhole principle in disguise.

Step by step.

  1. If f is injective, its n inputs give n distinct outputs inside an n-element codomain, so every element of B is used: f is also surjective, hence bijective. (A) is TRUE.
  2. If f is surjective, all n elements of B are hit; n hits from n inputs with no repeats is impossible unless each output is hit exactly once. So f is injective, hence bijective. (B) is TRUE.
  3. (C) is FALSE: with A = B = {1, 2}, the constant map f ≡ 1 is a function but not bijective.
  4. A bijection has an inverse: f⁻¹(y) is the unique x with f(x) = y. (D) is TRUE.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Reading "injective implies bijective" as a universal law. It holds only because |A| = |B| is finite; drop either hypothesis and it fails.

DM-FUN1-Q04MCQhard

Let f : ℝ → ℝ be defined by f(x) = x / (x² + 1). Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. f is injective but not surjective.
  2. f is surjective but not injective.
  3. f is neither injective nor surjective.
  4. f is bijective.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Injectivity is destroyed by a single collision f(a) = f(b) with a ≠ b. Surjectivity onto ℝ is destroyed by showing the range is bounded.

Step by step.

  1. Collision: f(2) = 2/5 and f(1/2) = (1/2)/(5/4) = 2/5. Since 2 ≠ 1/2, f is not injective.
  2. In general f(x) = f(1/x) for x ≠ 0, so every value away from 0 is taken at least twice.
  3. Range: by AM–GM, x² + 1 ≥ 2|x|, so |f(x)| ≤ 1/2, with equality at x = ±1.
  4. Values such as 1 lie outside [−1/2, 1/2], so f is not surjective onto ℝ.
  5. Therefore f is neither injective nor surjective.

Answer: Option (C) — neither injective nor surjective.

Common misconception. Testing injectivity only with integers, or assuming a bounded, symmetric-looking curve must still be one-to-one. The symmetry f(x) = f(1/x) is exactly what breaks injectivity.

DM-FUN1-Q05NATmedium

Let f : ℝ → ℝ be defined by f(x) = x² − 4x + 7. How many real numbers x satisfy f(x) = 3?
(Enter an integer.)

Answer: 1

Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Solving f(x) = c is solving a quadratic; the number of solutions is the number of distinct real roots, which the discriminant decides.

Step by step.

  1. Set x² − 4x + 7 = 3.
  2. Rearrange: x² − 4x + 4 = 0.
  3. Factor: (x − 2)² = 0, so x = 2 is a double root.
  4. The discriminant is 16 − 16 = 0, confirming exactly one distinct real solution.

Answer: 1

Common misconception. Counting the double root twice and answering 2. "How many real numbers x" asks for distinct solutions, so a repeated root counts once.

DM-FUN2-Q01MCQeasy

Let ℕ = {0, 1, 2, …} and let f : ℕ → ℕ be defined by f(n) = n + 5. Which one of the following describes f correctly?

  1. f is bijective.
  2. f is injective but not surjective.
  3. f is surjective but not injective.
  4. f is neither injective nor surjective.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A shift of the natural numbers is one-to-one, but the first few codomain values are simply never produced. Injectivity and surjectivity are separate tests and a shift passes only the first.

Step by step.

  1. If f(a) = f(b) then a + 5 = b + 5, so a = b: f is injective.
  2. The image is {5, 6, 7, …}: the values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 are never attained.
  3. So f is not surjective, and it is injective but not surjective.

Answer: Option (B) — injective, not surjective.

Common misconception. Students see a bijection of ℤ (namely n ↦ n + 5) and assume the same map is a bijection of ℕ. Shifting destroys surjectivity because ℕ has a first element and nothing maps onto the bottom five values.

DM-FUN2-Q02MCQmedium

Let f : ℝ → ℝ be defined by f(x) = x³ − x. Which one of the following describes f correctly?

  1. f is bijective.
  2. f is injective but not surjective.
  3. f is surjective but not injective.
  4. f is neither injective nor surjective.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. An odd-degree polynomial has full range ℝ (surjective), but it is injective only if it is monotone. A cubic with two turning points folds back on itself and therefore repeats values.

Step by step.

  1. f(0) = 0 and f(1) = 0, so two different inputs share an output: f is not injective.
  2. f′(x) = 3x² − 1, which vanishes at x = ±1/√3; these are the two turning points.
  3. As x → +∞, f(x) → +∞ and as x → −∞, f(x) → −∞; being continuous, f takes every real value, so it is surjective.
  4. Hence f is surjective but not injective.

Answer: Option (C) — surjective, not injective.

Common misconception. Assuming an odd-degree polynomial is automatically a bijection. Odd degree guarantees surjectivity only; injectivity needs monotonicity, which x³ − x lacks.

DM-FUN2-Q03MSQeasy

Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. f : ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = x³ is bijective.
  2. f : ℤ → ℤ, f(n) = n² is injective.
  3. f : ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = eˣ is injective.
  4. f : ℝ → [0, ∞), f(x) = x² is surjective.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Each option tests one side of the injective/surjective split on a specific codomain. Changing the codomain changes surjectivity; changing the domain changes injectivity.

Step by step.

  1. (A) x³ is strictly increasing on ℝ, so it is injective; it is continuous with limits ±∞, so its range is ℝ and it is surjective. TRUE.
  2. (B) f(1) = f(−1) = 1, so two inputs share an output. FALSE.
  3. (C) eˣ is strictly increasing, hence injective. (It is not surjective onto ℝ, but the option claims only injectivity.) TRUE.
  4. (D) For every y ≥ 0, f(√y) = y, so the codomain [0, ∞) is fully covered. TRUE.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Rejecting (C) because eˣ misses the negative numbers. Surjectivity is not being claimed there — and rejecting (D) because x² is not injective on ℝ. Each option names one property only.

DM-FUN2-Q04MCQhard

Let f : ℝ → ℝ be defined by f(x) = x + sin x. Which one of the following describes f correctly?

  1. f is injective but not surjective.
  2. f is surjective but not injective.
  3. f is bijective.
  4. f is neither injective nor surjective.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A differentiable function is strictly increasing when its derivative is non-negative and vanishes only at isolated points. A strictly increasing continuous function with infinite limits at both ends is a bijection of ℝ.

Step by step.

  1. f′(x) = 1 + cos x ≥ 0 for all x, and f′(x) = 0 only at x = (2k+1)π, a discrete set with no interval in between.
  2. So f is strictly increasing: x₁ < x₂ implies f(x₁) < f(x₂). Hence f is injective.
  3. As x → +∞, x + sin x ≥ x − 1 → +∞; as x → −∞, x + sin x ≤ x + 1 → −∞.
  4. f is continuous, so by the intermediate value theorem it takes every real value: f is surjective.
  5. Injective and surjective, therefore bijective.

Answer: Option (C) — bijective.

Common misconception. Because sin x oscillates, students expect f to oscillate too and to be non-injective. The linear term dominates: the derivative 1 + cos x never becomes negative, so the function never turns around.

DM-FUN2-Q05NATmedium

How many of the following six functions f : ℝ → ℝ are bijections?f₁(x) = 2x + 1, f₂(x) = x², f₃(x) = x³, f₄(x) = |x|, f₅(x) = eˣ, f₆(x) = x³ − x(Enter an integer.)

Answer: 2

Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A bijection of ℝ onto ℝ must be both one-to-one and onto. Even-degree powers and absolute values fold the line; the exponential escapes the negative range; a cubic with turning points folds locally.

Step by step.

  1. f₁(x) = 2x + 1: linear with non-zero slope, range ℝ. Bijection. (1)
  2. f₂(x) = x²: f(1) = f(−1) = 1, so not injective; range [0, ∞), so not surjective either. Not a bijection.
  3. f₃(x) = x³: strictly increasing, range ℝ. Bijection. (2)
  4. f₄(x) = |x|: f(1) = f(−1) = 1, not injective; range [0, ∞), not surjective. No.
  5. f₅(x) = eˣ: injective, but the range is (0, ∞), so −1 is never attained. Not onto.
  6. f₆(x) = x³ − x: f(0) = f(1) = 0, so not injective (it is onto). No.
  7. Total: f₁ and f₃ only, so the answer is 2.

Answer: 2

Common misconception. Counting eˣ as a bijection because it has an inverse function ln x. The inverse exists on (0, ∞) only — eˣ : ℝ → ℝ is injective but not onto, so it is not a bijection of ℝ.

Composition & inverses 10
DM-FUN1-Q06MCQeasy

Let f, g : ℝ → ℝ with f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x². Then (f ∘ g)(x) equals

  1. 4x² + 12x + 9
  2. 2x² + 3
  3. 4x² + 3
  4. 2x² + 3x
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)): the right-hand function acts first, and its output becomes the input of the left-hand function.

Step by step.

  1. (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)) = f(x²).
  2. Substitute x² into f(u) = 2u + 3: f(x²) = 2x² + 3.

Answer: Option (B) — 2x² + 3.

Common misconception. Applying f first. Composition is read right to left: in f ∘ g, g goes first.

DM-FUN1-Q07MCQmedium

Let f : A → B and g : B → C. Suppose g ∘ f : A → C is injective. Which one of the following must be TRUE?

  1. f is injective.
  2. g is injective.
  3. f is surjective.
  4. g is surjective.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Injectivity of a composite forces injectivity of the first map applied, but says nothing about the second.

Step by step.

  1. Suppose f(a₁) = f(a₂). Applying g gives g(f(a₁)) = g(f(a₂)), i.e. (g∘f)(a₁) = (g∘f)(a₂).
  2. Injectivity of g ∘ f then gives a₁ = a₂. Hence f is injective. (A) holds.
  3. Counterexample for g: A = {1}, B = {p, q}, C = {r}, f(1) = p, g(p) = g(q) = r. Then g ∘ f is injective but g is not, so (B) fails.
  4. Surjectivity is untouched: with A = B = C = {1} and identity maps everything is injective and surjective; with B = {p, q} above, f is not surjective, so (C) fails.

Answer: Option (A) — f must be injective.

Common misconception. Concluding that g is injective because g ∘ f is. g only has to be injective on the image of f, not on all of B.

DM-FUN1-Q08MSQeasy

Let f : A → B and g : B → C. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. If f and g are both injective, then g ∘ f is injective.
  2. If f and g are both surjective, then g ∘ f is surjective.
  3. If g ∘ f is surjective, then g is surjective.
  4. If g ∘ f is injective, then g is injective.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Composition preserves both injectivity and surjectivity when both factors have the property, and the composite can also pass a property back to one factor.

Step by step.

  1. (A) If (g∘f)(a₁) = (g∘f)(a₂), injectivity of g gives f(a₁) = f(a₂) and injectivity of f gives a₁ = a₂. TRUE.
  2. (B) Take any c ∈ C. Surjectivity of g gives b ∈ B with g(b) = c; surjectivity of f gives a ∈ A with f(a) = b. Then (g∘f)(a) = c. TRUE.
  3. (C) The image of g ∘ f is g(f(A)) ⊆ g(B). If g(f(A)) = C then certainly g(B) = C. TRUE.
  4. (D) FALSE: take A = {1}, B = {p, q}, C = {r}, f(1) = p, g(p) = g(q) = r. Then g∘f is injective but g is not.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Assuming every property is inherited in both directions. Composition preserves injective/injective and surjective/surjective forwards, but passes a property back to only one factor.

DM-FUN1-Q09MCQhard

Let f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = x² be functions on ℝ, and put h = g ∘ f, k = f ∘ g. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. h = k as functions.
  2. The equation h(x) = k(x) holds for exactly one real x.
  3. Both h and k are injective.
  4. k ∘ h = h ∘ k as functions.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Two composites of the same pair of functions generally differ; comparing them means writing both in closed form and solving, and remembering that x² is not injective.

Step by step.

  1. h(x) = g(f(x)) = (x + 1)² and k(x) = f(g(x)) = x² + 1. They are different functions, so (A) is false.
  2. h(x) = k(x) ⇔ x² + 2x + 1 = x² + 1 ⇔ 2x = 0 ⇔ x = 0. Exactly one solution, so (B) is true.
  3. k(1) = k(−1) = 2, so k is not injective and (C) is false.
  4. k(h(x)) = ((x+1)²)² + 1 = (x+1)⁴ + 1 while h(k(x)) = (x² + 1 + 1)² = (x² + 2)². At x = 0 these are 2 and 4, so (D) is false.

Answer: Option (B) — exactly one real solution, x = 0.

Common misconception. Assuming g ∘ f = f ∘ g for "simple" functions, or that composing twice is automatically commutative. Composition is associative but almost never commutative.

DM-FUN1-Q10NATmedium

Let f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = 3x + 1 be bijections on ℝ. Find the value of (f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹)(16).
(Enter an integer.)

Answer: 2

Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. To evaluate f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹, apply the right-hand inverse first: undo g, then undo f. Equivalently use (g ∘ f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹.

Step by step.

  1. Inverses: f⁻¹(y) = (y − 1)/2 and g⁻¹(y) = (y − 1)/3.
  2. Apply g⁻¹ first: g⁻¹(16) = (16 − 1)/3 = 5.
  3. Then apply f⁻¹: f⁻¹(5) = (5 − 1)/2 = 2.
  4. Check with the other route: (g ∘ f)(x) = 3(2x + 1) + 1 = 6x + 4, and 6x + 4 = 16 gives x = 2. Both routes agree.

Answer: 2

Common misconception. Applying f⁻¹ first, which computes (g⁻¹ ∘ f⁻¹)(16) = g⁻¹(7.5) = 13/6 — a different number. In f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹ the function written on the right acts first, exactly as in ordinary composition.

DM-FUN2-Q06MCQeasy

Let f(x) = x + 2 and g(x) = 3x be functions on ℝ. Then (g ∘ f)(x) equals

  1. 3x + 2
  2. 3x + 6
  3. 3x² + 6x
  4. x + 6
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Composition applies the right-hand function first: (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)). Substitute f(x) into g, not the other way round.

Step by step.

  1. Compute f first: f(x) = x + 2.
  2. Feed that value into g: g(x + 2) = 3(x + 2).
  3. Expand: 3x + 6.

Answer: Option (B) — 3x + 6.

Common misconception. Reading (g ∘ f)(x) left to right as g then f. The composition symbol is applied right to left: the function nearest the argument runs first.

DM-FUN2-Q07MCQmedium

Let f(x) = x² and g(x) = √x both be defined on [0, ∞) with codomain [0, ∞). Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. (f ∘ g)(x) = |x| for all x ≥ 0.
  2. f and g are inverse functions of each other on [0, ∞).
  3. (g ∘ f)(x) is undefined for x ≥ 0.
  4. There is some x ≥ 0 with (f ∘ g)(x) ≠ (g ∘ f)(x).
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Two functions are inverses when both compositions are the identity on the relevant domains. Restricting x² to [0, ∞) is exactly what makes √x a genuine inverse.

Step by step.

  1. (f ∘ g)(x) = (√x)² = x for every x ≥ 0, since √x ≥ 0.
  2. (g ∘ f)(x) = √(x²) = |x| = x for every x ≥ 0.
  3. Both compositions are the identity on [0, ∞), so f and g are mutually inverse there.

Answer: Option (B) — they are inverses of each other on [0, ∞).

Common misconception. Quoting √(x²) = |x| and concluding the two compositions differ. That identity is about all real x; on the restricted domain [0, ∞) we have |x| = x, so the compositions coincide.

DM-FUN2-Q08MSQeasy

Which of the following statements about composition and inverses are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Composition is associative: (f ∘ g) ∘ h = f ∘ (g ∘ h) whenever all the compositions are defined.
  2. f ∘ g = g ∘ f whenever both compositions are defined.
  3. If f : A → B is a bijection, then f ∘ f⁻¹ is the identity on B.
  4. If f and g are bijections, then (f ∘ g)⁻¹ = g⁻¹ ∘ f⁻¹.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Composition behaves like multiplication of functions: associative, generally not commutative, and the inverse of a product reverses the order.

Step by step.

  1. (A) Both sides send x to f(g(h(x))). TRUE.
  2. (B) Take f(x) = x + 1, g(x) = x². Then (f∘g)(1) = 2 while (g∘f)(1) = 4. FALSE.
  3. (C) (f ∘ f⁻¹)(y) = f(f⁻¹(y)) = y for every y ∈ B. TRUE.
  4. (D) (f ∘ g)(g⁻¹ ∘ f⁻¹) = f ∘ (g ∘ g⁻¹) ∘ f⁻¹ = f ∘ f⁻¹ = identity, and similarly on the other side. TRUE.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Assuming that because matrix multiplication is associative and non-commutative in the same way, function composition behaves identically in every respect — in particular, that the inverse of f ∘ g is f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹. The order must reverse.

DM-FUN2-Q09MCQhard

Let f : ℤ → ℤ be f(x) = 2x and g : ℤ → ℤ be g(x) = ⌊x/2⌋. Which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. f and g are inverse bijections of each other.
  2. g ∘ f is the identity on ℤ, but f ∘ g is not; and f is not surjective.
  3. Both g ∘ f and f ∘ g are the identity on ℤ.
  4. g ∘ f is not injective.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. One composition being the identity forces only one of the two functions to be injective and the other surjective. Two functions are mutual inverses only when both compositions are the identity.

Step by step.

  1. (g ∘ f)(x) = ⌊2x/2⌋ = ⌊x⌋ = x for every integer x. So g ∘ f is the identity on ℤ.
  2. (f ∘ g)(x) = 2⌊x/2⌋, which equals x when x is even and x − 1 when x is odd. So f ∘ g is not the identity.
  3. Indeed f ∘ g is not injective: (f ∘ g)(0) = 0 and (f ∘ g)(1) = 0.
  4. f(x) = 2x has image 2ℤ, so odd integers are never attained: f is not surjective.
  5. Hence (B) holds; (A) and (C) fail because the second composition is not the identity.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Concluding from g ∘ f = id that f and g are inverses. A one-sided identity gives f injective and g surjective only — here f misses the odd integers and g identifies 2k with 2k + 1, so neither is a bijection.

DM-FUN2-Q10NATmedium

Let f(x) = 2x − 1 and g(x) = x + 3 be bijections on ℝ. Find (g ∘ f)⁻¹(8).(Enter an integer.)

Answer: 3

Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Two routes give the same answer: invert the composite directly, or use (g ∘ f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹ and work backwards through g then f.

Step by step.

  1. First find the composite: (g ∘ f)(x) = g(2x − 1) = (2x − 1) + 3 = 2x + 2.
  2. Solve 2x + 2 = 8, giving 2x = 6 and x = 3.
  3. Check by the inverse-order route: g⁻¹(y) = y − 3 gives g⁻¹(8) = 5; f⁻¹(y) = (y + 1)/2 gives f⁻¹(5) = 3. Both agree.

Answer: 3

Common misconception. Evaluating g⁻¹ first and then f⁻¹ the wrong way round, i.e. computing f⁻¹(g⁻¹(8)) with f⁻¹ applied first. The composite (g ∘ f)⁻¹ is f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹, so g⁻¹ acts first.

Counting functions 10
DM-FUN1-Q11MCQeasy

Let |A| = 4 and |B| = 3. How many functions f : A → B are there?

  1. 12
  2. 24
  3. 81
  4. 64
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A function A → B is an independent choice of one codomain element for each domain element, so the count is |B|^|A|.

Step by step.

  1. Each of the 4 elements of A may map to any of the 3 elements of B.
  2. The choices are independent, so multiply: 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 3⁴ = 81.

Answer: Option (C) — 81.

Common misconception. Swapping the exponent: the domain size is the exponent, the codomain size is the base.

DM-FUN1-Q12MCQmedium

Let |A| = 4 and |B| = 5. How many injective functions f : A → B are there?

  1. 20
  2. 120
  3. 625
  4. 24
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. An injective function picks distinct images for the domain elements in turn, so the count is a falling factorial |B|(|B|−1)…(|B|−|A|+1).

Step by step.

  1. The first element of A has 5 possible images.
  2. The second must avoid that one: 4 choices. The third: 3 choices. The fourth: 2 choices.
  3. Multiply: 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 = 120.

Answer: Option (B) — 120.

Common misconception. Using |B|^|A| and forgetting the distinctness constraint, or using P(5,5) instead of P(5,4).

DM-FUN1-Q13MSQeasy

Let |A| = 3 and |B| = 4. Which of the following counts are correct? (Select all that apply.)

  1. There are 64 functions f : A → B.
  2. There are 24 injective functions f : A → B.
  3. There are 0 surjective functions f : A → B.
  4. There are 24 bijections f : A → B.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Counts follow the size comparison: all functions |B|^|A|, injective P(|B|,|A|), surjective 0 whenever |A| < |B|, bijections 0 whenever |A| ≠ |B|.

Step by step.

  1. All functions: 4³ = 64. (A) TRUE.
  2. Injective: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24. (B) TRUE.
  3. Surjective: 3 inputs can hit at most 3 of the 4 codomain elements, so none. (C) TRUE.
  4. Bijections require equal sizes; 3 ≠ 4, so there are 0, not 24. (D) FALSE.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Equating "injective count" with "bijection count". They coincide only when the two sets have equal size.

DM-FUN1-Q14MCQhard

Let |A| = 5 and |B| = 3. How many surjective functions f : A → B are there?

  1. 90
  2. 125
  3. 150
  4. 243
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Count onto maps by inclusion–exclusion over the codomain elements that are missed: Σ (−1)^k C(n,k) (n−k)^m for m inputs and n targets.

Step by step.

  1. Total functions: 3⁵ = 243.
  2. Subtract those missing at least one target. Missing a fixed target leaves 2⁵ = 32 functions, and there are C(3,1) = 3 choices of the missed target: 3 × 32 = 96.
  3. Add back the double subtractions. Missing two fixed targets leaves 1⁵ = 1 function, with C(3,2) = 3 such pairs: 3.
  4. Nothing misses all three targets. So the count is 243 − 96 + 3 = 150.

Answer: Option (C) — 150.

Common misconception. Using S(m,n) alone. The Stirling number counts partitions of the domain, so the number of onto maps is n! · S(m,n) = 6 × 25 = 150; forgetting the n! factor (or using a wrong Stirling value) is the usual error.

DM-FUN1-Q15NATmedium

How many bijections are there from a set with 6 elements onto itself?
(Enter an integer.)

Answer: 720

Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A bijection from a finite set onto itself is a permutation of its elements, so the count is n!.

Step by step.

  1. Choose the image of element 1: 6 ways.
  2. Choose the image of element 2 from what is left: 5 ways, and so on down to 1 way for the last element.
  3. Multiply: 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 720.

Answer: 720

Common misconception. Counting 6⁶ (all functions) or 2⁶. A bijection must use each element exactly once, which is a permutation, not an arbitrary assignment.

DM-FUN2-Q11MCQeasy

Let |A| = 3 and |B| = 5. How many functions f : A → B are there?

  1. 15
  2. 125
  3. 243
  4. 60
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A function makes an independent choice of image for each of the |A| domain elements, with |B| options each time. The count is |B|^|A|, not |A|·|B|.

Step by step.

  1. Each of the 3 elements of A independently picks one of the 5 elements of B.
  2. By the product rule the number of functions is 5 × 5 × 5 = 5³.
  3. 5³ = 125.

Answer: Option (B) — 125.

Common misconception. Confusing |B|^|A| with |A|^|B|. The exponent is the size of the domain, because each domain element makes a choice.

DM-FUN2-Q12MCQmedium

Let |A| = 5 and |B| = 3. How many injective functions f : A → B are there?

  1. 243
  2. 0
  3. 120
  4. 60
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. An injection needs at least as many codomain points as domain points. When |A| > |B| the pigeonhole principle makes an injection impossible, so the count is 0.

Step by step.

  1. An injective f would send 5 distinct domain elements to 5 distinct codomain elements.
  2. But B has only 3 elements, so 5 distinct images cannot fit.
  3. By the pigeonhole principle no injective map exists; the count is 0.

Answer: Option (B) — 0.

Common misconception. Mechanically applying P(|B|, |A|) and getting a negative or nonsensical product. The formula P(n, r) is defined only for r ≤ n; here r = 5 > n = 3, so the honest answer is 0.

DM-FUN2-Q13MSQeasy

Let |A| = 2 and |B| = 4. Which of the following counts are correct? (Select all that apply.)

  1. There are 16 functions f : A → B.
  2. There are 12 injective functions f : A → B.
  3. There are 0 surjective functions f : A → B.
  4. There are 12 bijections f : A → B.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The four counts follow from the size comparison: |B|^|A| functions, P(|B|, |A|) injections, and no surjection or bijection when |A| < |B|.

Step by step.

  1. Functions: 4² = 16. (A) TRUE.
  2. Injections: P(4, 2) = 4 × 3 = 12. (B) TRUE.
  3. Surjections: two inputs can hit at most two codomain elements, so with |B| = 4 at least two elements are missed. Count 0. (C) TRUE.
  4. Bijections require |A| = |B|; here 2 ≠ 4, so the count is 0, not 12. (D) FALSE.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Reading 'injective' and 'bijective' as interchangeable on unequal sets. With |A| < |B| an injection exists but can never be onto, so no bijection exists.

DM-FUN2-Q14MCQhard

Let |A| = 6 and |B| = 3. How many surjective functions f : A → B are there?

  1. 540
  2. 729
  3. 90
  4. 243
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Count the complement with inclusion–exclusion: subtract the maps that miss at least one codomain element, add back the double-counted ones. The answer is Σ(−1)ᵏ C(n,k)(n−k)^m for m = |A|, n = |B|.

Step by step.

  1. Total functions: 3⁶ = 729.
  2. Maps missing a fixed element of B: 2⁶ = 64 each, and there are C(3,1) = 3 of them: subtract 3 × 64 = 192.
  3. Maps missing two fixed elements (i.e. constant maps): 1⁶ = 1 each, C(3,2) = 3 of them: add back 3.
  4. Surjective count = 729 − 192 + 3 = 540.

Answer: Option (A) — 540.

Common misconception. Computing 3! · S(6,3) correctly as 540 but stopping at 3⁶ − 3·2⁶ = 537 and forgetting the +3 correction. Inclusion–exclusion must alternate signs all the way down.

DM-FUN2-Q15NATmedium

How many functions f : {1, 2, 3, 4} → {1, 2, 3, 4} are NOT bijections?(Enter an integer.)

Answer: 232

Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Count all functions on a 4-element set and subtract the bijections. A function from a finite set to itself is a bijection exactly when it is a permutation.

Step by step.

  1. Total functions: 4⁴ = 256.
  2. Bijections on 4 elements: 4! = 24.
  3. Non-bijections: 256 − 24 = 232.

Answer: 232

Common misconception. Answering 256 − 4 = 252, subtracting the number of elements instead of the number of permutations. There are 24 bijections, not 4.

Pigeonhole principle 10
DM-FUN1-Q16MCQeasy

What is the minimum number of people in a room that guarantees at least three of them were born in the same month?

  1. 13
  2. 24
  3. 25
  4. 27
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. To force k + 1 objects into one of m boxes, you need km + 1 objects: with only km you could place exactly k in every box.

Step by step.

  1. Here m = 12 months and we want k + 1 = 3, so k = 2.
  2. The bound is 2 × 12 + 1 = 25.
  3. Sharpness: 24 people can be spread with exactly 2 per month, so 24 is not enough. With 25 people some month receives at least ⌈25/12⌉ = 3.

Answer: Option (C) — 25.

Common misconception. Answering 24 because "2 per month is 24". That is exactly the configuration to be avoided; the guarantee needs one more.

DM-FUN1-Q17MCQmedium

Let f be a function from a set with 10 elements into a set with 9 elements. Which one of the following must be TRUE?

  1. f is injective.
  2. Some element of the codomain is the image of at least two domain elements.
  3. f is surjective.
  4. Exactly one codomain element is the image of exactly two domain elements.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Pigeonhole: 10 objects in 9 boxes force some box to hold at least two. It says nothing about which box, or about how the rest are distributed.

Step by step.

  1. The 10 domain elements are assigned to 9 codomain elements.
  2. If every codomain element were the image of at most one element, the image would contain 10 distinct values inside a 9-element set — impossible.
  3. So some codomain element is hit at least twice. (B) holds.
  4. Nothing forces surjectivity: the map could send all 10 elements to one value and leave 8 values unused. So (C) fails, and (A) fails too.
  5. Nothing forces the excess to be exactly 2: f could send 3 elements to one value. So (D) fails.

Answer: Option (B) — some codomain element is hit at least twice.

Common misconception. Strengthening the conclusion from "at least two" to "exactly two". The pigeonhole principle gives an inequality, not a distribution.

DM-FUN1-Q18MSQeasy

Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. In any group of 13 people, at least two share a birth month.
  2. In any group of 25 people, at least three share a birth month.
  3. In any group of 24 people, at least three share a birth month.
  4. If 11 numbers are chosen from {1, 2, …, 20}, two of them are consecutive.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Each claim is a pigeonhole count: identify the objects, the boxes, and how many objects force a given occupancy.

Step by step.

  1. (A) 13 people, 12 months: ⌈13/12⌉ = 2, so some month holds at least two. TRUE.
  2. (B) 25 people: ⌈25/12⌉ = 3. TRUE.
  3. (C) 24 people can occupy the 12 months exactly two at a time, so three is not forced. FALSE.
  4. (D) Split {1, …, 20} into the 10 pairs {1,2}, {3,4}, …, {19,20}. Choosing 11 numbers means two come from the same pair, and those two are consecutive. TRUE.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Treating 24 as "close enough" to force three, and forgetting to build the boxes in (D). For (D) the boxes are the consecutive pairs, not the numbers themselves.

DM-FUN1-Q19MCQhard

Given any 5 integers, which one of the following is guaranteed?

  1. Some three of them have a sum divisible by 3.
  2. Some two of them have a sum divisible by 3.
  3. Some four of them have a sum divisible by 3.
  4. Their total sum is divisible by 3.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Work modulo 3. Only the residues matter, and there are just three of them, so a short case analysis on how the five residues are distributed settles everything.

Step by step.

  1. Reduce the five integers modulo 3, giving five residues in {0, 1, 2}.
  2. Case 1: some residue class contains at least three of them. Three integers with the same residue r sum to 3r ≡ 0 (mod 3). Done.
  3. Case 2: no class has three. With five residues over three classes, the counts must be (2, 2, 1) in some order.
  4. Then one element has each residue 0, 1, 2, and 0 + 1 + 2 = 3 ≡ 0 (mod 3). Done.
  5. So a suitable triple always exists, and (A) is guaranteed.

Answer: Option (A) — some three have a sum divisible by 3.

Common misconception. Stopping after Case 1. The interesting case is the "balanced" distribution (2, 2, 1), where no class is large but one element of each residue still gives a multiple of 3.

DM-FUN1-Q20NATmedium

What is the smallest number n such that among any n integers there are always two whose difference is divisible by 9?
(Enter an integer.)

Answer: 10

Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. "Difference divisible by 9" means the two integers are congruent modulo 9, so the boxes are the 9 residue classes and the objects are the chosen integers.

Step by step.

  1. Two integers differ by a multiple of 9 exactly when they share a residue modulo 9. There are 9 residues, i.e. 9 boxes.
  2. With 9 integers we can pick one from each class, e.g. 0, 1, …, 8, and no two share a residue. So n = 9 is not enough.
  3. With 10 integers, two must fall in the same class, and their difference is divisible by 9.
  4. Hence the smallest such n is 10.

Answer: 10

Common misconception. Answering 9 because there are 9 residue classes. Nine objects can occupy nine boxes one each; the guarantee needs one more object than there are boxes.

DM-FUN2-Q16MCQeasy

What is the minimum number of students needed to guarantee that at least two of them were born on the same day of the week?

  1. 7
  2. 8
  3. 14
  4. 53
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. With m boxes, m + 1 objects force a collision. The days of the week are the 7 boxes.

Step by step.

  1. Treat the 7 weekdays as boxes and the students as objects.
  2. With 7 students it is possible for each to fall in a different box — no guarantee.
  3. With 8 students, 8 > 7 forces two into the same box by the pigeonhole principle.

Answer: Option (B) — 8.

Common misconception. Answering 7 by analogy with '7 days'. The guarantee needs one more object than there are boxes, so the threshold is 7 + 1 = 8.

DM-FUN2-Q17MCQmedium

A drawer holds 10 red, 10 blue and 10 green socks. Drawing in the dark, what is the smallest number of socks that guarantees a matching pair (two of the same colour)?

  1. 3
  2. 4
  3. 11
  4. 21
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The worst case before a collision is one sock of every colour. One more sock than there are colours forces a repeat.

Step by step.

  1. There are 3 colours, so 3 boxes.
  2. Worst case: draw one red, one blue and one green — 3 socks, still no pair.
  3. The 4th sock must repeat one of the three colours, giving a matching pair.

Answer: Option (B) — 4.

Common misconception. Using the 10 socks per colour as the box count. The boxes here are colours (3), not socks. Separately, guaranteeing a specific colour does need 21.

DM-FUN2-Q18MSQeasy

Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Among any 5 integers, two leave the same remainder on division by 4.
  2. Among any 6 integers, two differ by a multiple of 5.
  3. Among any 4 integers, two differ by a multiple of 4.
  4. Among any 13 integers, two leave the same remainder on division by 12.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Two integers differ by a multiple of k exactly when they share a remainder mod k. So the question is always: how many objects can share k boxes before a collision is forced?

Step by step.

  1. (A) 5 objects, 4 residues: 5 > 4, so a collision is forced. TRUE.
  2. (B) 6 objects, 5 residues mod 5: 6 > 5, forced. TRUE.
  3. (C) 4 objects, 4 residues mod 4: the integers 0, 1, 2, 3 occupy all four residues with no repeat. FALSE.
  4. (D) 13 objects, 12 residues: 13 > 12, forced. TRUE.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Assuming any k integers must collide mod k. The threshold is k + 1; with exactly k integers a clean one-per-class arrangement always exists.

DM-FUN2-Q19MCQhard

Each cell of a 10 × 10 grid is coloured with one of 4 colours. Which one of the following must be TRUE?

  1. Some colour is used on at least 25 cells.
  2. Some colour is used on at least 26 cells.
  3. Every colour is used on exactly 25 cells.
  4. No colour is used on more than 30 cells.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. With 100 objects in 4 boxes, the average is 25, so the largest box has at least ⌈100/4⌉ = 25. The bound is tight: a perfectly even split attains it, so no larger universal guarantee is possible.

Step by step.

  1. There are 100 cells and 4 colours: 100 objects, 4 boxes.
  2. If every colour were used on at most 24 cells, the total would be at most 4 × 24 = 96 < 100, a contradiction.
  3. So some colour covers at least 25 cells. (A) is TRUE.
  4. Colour the grid in four 5 × 5 blocks of 25 cells each: no colour then reaches 26, so (B) is not guaranteed.
  5. An uneven split such as 40, 20, 20, 20 refutes (C), and a monochromatic grid refutes (D).

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Upgrading 'at least 25' to 'at least 26'. The generalised pigeonhole principle gives ⌈N/k⌉ = ⌈100/4⌉ = 25 exactly, and 25 is attained, so any larger claim is false.

DM-FUN2-Q20NATmedium

In a class of 40 students, what is the largest k such that some birth month is guaranteed to contain at least k of them?(Enter an integer.)

Answer: 4

Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The generalised pigeonhole principle guarantees a box with at least ⌈N/m⌉ objects, and that bound is the largest guaranteed value.

Step by step.

  1. 40 students, 12 months: ⌈40/12⌉ = ⌈3.33…⌉ = 4.
  2. So some month holds at least 4 students — the guarantee cannot fail.
  3. It is tight: 40 = 12 × 3 + 4, so 4 months can hold 4 students and the remaining 8 months 3 each, with no month reaching 5.

Answer: 4

Common misconception. Rounding down to 3 with ⌊40/12⌋. The pigeonhole principle rounds up: if every month held at most 3, only 36 students could be placed.

Floor, ceiling & recursion 10
DM-FUN1-Q21MCQeasy

For a real number x, the value of ⌈x⌉ − ⌊x⌋ is

  1. always 0
  2. 0 when x is an integer, and 1 otherwise
  3. always 1
  4. 0 when x is an integer, and −1 otherwise
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. ⌊x⌋ is the largest integer not exceeding x; ⌈x⌉ is the smallest integer not less than x. Their difference measures the fractional part.

Step by step.

  1. If x ∈ ℤ, then ⌊x⌋ = ⌈x⌉ = x, so the difference is 0.
  2. If x ∉ ℤ, write x = k + f with k ∈ ℤ and 0 < f < 1. Then ⌊x⌋ = k and ⌈x⌉ = k + 1.
  3. So the difference is 1 exactly for non-integers.
  4. Check: x = 2.3 gives 3 − 2 = 1; x = −2.3 gives −2 − (−3) = 1; x = 5 gives 0.

Answer: Option (B) — 0 for integers, 1 otherwise.

Common misconception. Handling negative numbers wrongly. For x = −2.3, ⌊x⌋ = −3 and ⌈x⌉ = −2; the difference is still 1, not −1.

DM-FUN1-Q22MCQmedium

How many integers from 1 to 1000 (both inclusive) are divisible by neither 3 nor 5?

  1. 466
  2. 533
  3. 534
  4. 600
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Counting "neither" is inclusion–exclusion on the complement: subtract the multiples of 3 and of 5, then add back the multiples of 15 that were removed twice.

Step by step.

  1. Multiples of 3 up to 1000: ⌊1000/3⌋ = 333.
  2. Multiples of 5: ⌊1000/5⌋ = 200.
  3. Multiples of 15 (counted in both lists): ⌊1000/15⌋ = 66.
  4. Divisible by 3 or 5: 333 + 200 − 66 = 467.
  5. Neither: 1000 − 467 = 533.

Answer: Option (B) — 533.

Common misconception. Subtracting 333 and 200 and stopping: the 66 multiples of 15 get removed twice, so the total of "divisible by 3 or 5" is overstated and the "neither" count is understated by 66.

DM-FUN1-Q23MSQeasy

Which of the following identities hold for ALL real numbers x and y? (Select all that apply.)

  1. ⌊−x⌋ = −⌈x⌉
  2. ⌈−x⌉ = −⌊x⌋
  3. ⌊x + ½⌋ = ⌈x⌉
  4. ⌊x⌋ + ⌊y⌋ ≤ ⌊x + y⌋
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Negation swaps floor and ceiling; floors add sub-additively, never super-additively.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: reflecting about 0 turns the greatest integer below x into the least integer above −x. Test x = 2.3: ⌊−2.3⌋ = −3 = −⌈2.3⌉.
  2. (B) True: the same reflection the other way. Test x = 2.3: ⌈−2.3⌉ = −2 = −⌊2.3⌋.
  3. (C) False: at x = 0.4, ⌊0.9⌋ = 0 but ⌈0.4⌉ = 1.
  4. (D) True: ⌊x⌋ ≤ x and ⌊y⌋ ≤ y, so ⌊x⌋ + ⌊y⌋ ≤ x + y; the left side is an integer, hence it is at most ⌊x + y⌋.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Believing ⌊x + y⌋ = ⌊x⌋ + ⌊y⌋. It can differ by 1 (take x = y = 0.6) but the left side is never smaller.

DM-FUN1-Q24MCQhard

Let f(0) = 1 and f(n) = f(⌊n/2⌋) + 1 for every integer n ≥ 1. Then f(1000) equals

  1. 10
  2. 11
  3. 12
  4. 13
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Unrolling a recurrence that halves its argument counts how many halvings are needed to reach 0, i.e. the number of bits of n plus one.

Step by step.

  1. f(1000) = f(500) + 1 = f(250) + 2 = f(125) + 3.
  2. f(125) = f(62) + 1, f(62) = f(31) + 1, f(31) = f(15) + 1, f(15) = f(7) + 1, f(7) = f(3) + 1, f(3) = f(1) + 1, f(1) = f(0) + 1 = 2.
  3. Working back up: f(3) = 3, f(7) = 4, f(15) = 5, f(31) = 6, f(62) = 7, f(125) = 8, f(250) = 9, f(500) = 10, f(1000) = 11.
  4. Closed form: f(n) = ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 2 for n ≥ 1. Here ⌊log₂ 1000⌋ = 9 since 2⁹ = 512 ≤ 1000 < 1024 = 2¹⁰, so f(1000) = 11.

Answer: Option (B) — 11.

Common misconception. Using log₂1000 ≈ 9.97 → 10 and then answering 10. The recurrence counts halvings with floor division, and the base case contributes the extra 1.

DM-FUN1-Q25NATmedium

A sequence is defined by T(1) = 1 and T(n) = T(⌊n/2⌋) + n for n ≥ 2. Find T(8).
(Enter an integer.)

Answer: 15

Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Unroll the recurrence from the top down, replacing each argument by its floor half until the base case is reached, then add the contributions on the way back up.

Step by step.

  1. T(8) = T(4) + 8.
  2. T(4) = T(2) + 4.
  3. T(2) = T(1) + 2 = 1 + 2 = 3.
  4. So T(4) = 3 + 4 = 7 and T(8) = 7 + 8 = 15.
  5. Check with the sum form: T(8) = 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15, since the arguments along the chain are the powers of two down to the base case.

Answer: 15

Common misconception. Adding the halved values (4 + 2 + 1) instead of the original arguments, which gives 8 rather than 15; in this recurrence the added term is n, the current argument.

DM-FUN2-Q21MCQeasy

For the real number x = −3.4, the value of ⌊x⌋ + ⌈x⌉ is

  1. −7
  2. −6
  3. 6
  4. 7
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. For negative arguments the floor rounds down (more negative) and the ceiling rounds up (towards zero). They are not symmetric about zero.

Step by step.

  1. ⌊−3.4⌋ is the greatest integer ≤ −3.4, namely −4.
  2. ⌈−3.4⌉ is the least integer ≥ −3.4, namely −3.
  3. Sum: −4 + (−3) = −7.

Answer: Option (A) — −7.

Common misconception. Truncating towards zero, i.e. reading ⌊−3.4⌋ as −3. Floor always moves left on the number line, so a negative non-integer floors to the next more negative integer.

DM-FUN2-Q22MCQmedium

How many integers n with 1 ≤ n ≤ 100 satisfy ⌊n/3⌋ = 12?

  1. 2
  2. 3
  3. 4
  4. 12
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. ⌊n/3⌋ = k exactly when k ≤ n/3 < k + 1, i.e. 3k ≤ n ≤ 3k + 2. Each value of k is attained by exactly 3 consecutive integers.

Step by step.

  1. ⌊n/3⌋ = 12 ⟺ 12 ≤ n/3 < 13 ⟺ 36 ≤ n < 39.
  2. The integers are 36, 37, 38.
  3. All three lie in 1 ≤ n ≤ 100, so the count is 3.

Answer: Option (B) — 3.

Common misconception. Reading ⌊n/3⌋ = 12 as n = 36 only. A floor value is attained on a whole block of three integers, and the right endpoint is excluded.

DM-FUN2-Q23MSQeasy

Which of the following hold for ALL real numbers x and y? (Select all that apply.)

  1. ⌈x⌉ ≥ x
  2. ⌊x⌋ ≤ x
  3. ⌊x⌋ + ⌊y⌋ = ⌊x + y⌋
  4. ⌈x⌉ + ⌈y⌉ ≥ ⌈x + y⌉
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Floor and ceiling bracket the argument: ⌊x⌋ ≤ x ≤ ⌈x⌉. Ceiling is superadditive and floor is subadditive; the floor identity fails whenever the fractional parts sum to 1 or more.

Step by step.

  1. (A) ⌈x⌉ is by definition an integer ≥ x. TRUE.
  2. (B) ⌊x⌋ is by definition an integer ≤ x. TRUE.
  3. (C) Take x = y = 0.5: ⌊0.5⌋ + ⌊0.5⌋ = 0 while ⌊1.0⌋ = 1. FALSE.
  4. (D) ⌈x⌉ ≥ x and ⌈y⌉ ≥ y, so ⌈x⌉ + ⌈y⌉ ≥ x + y. The left side is an integer, hence it is at least ⌈x + y⌉. TRUE.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Assuming floor distributes over addition. The correct one-way inequalities are ⌊x⌋ + ⌊y⌋ ≤ ⌊x + y⌋ and ⌈x⌉ + ⌈y⌉ ≥ ⌈x + y⌉; equality is not general.

DM-FUN2-Q24MCQhard

Let T(1) = 1 and T(n) = 2T(⌊n/2⌋) + n for n ≥ 2. Then T(8) equals

  1. 24
  2. 28
  3. 32
  4. 36
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Unroll a halving recurrence on a power of two: the argument halves each level, so only about log₂ n levels exist and the terms form a geometric series.

Step by step.

  1. T(1) = 1.
  2. T(2) = 2T(1) + 2 = 2 + 2 = 4.
  3. T(4) = 2T(2) + 4 = 8 + 4 = 12.
  4. T(8) = 2T(4) + 8 = 24 + 8 = 32.
  5. Cross-check with the closed form T(n) = n log₂ n + n for powers of two: 8 × 3 + 8 = 32, agreeing with the unrolling.

Answer: Option (C) — 32.

Common misconception. Plugging into the Master Theorem and reporting Θ(n log n) as though it were the value at n = 8. The asymptotic form hides constants; a numerical question needs the recurrence unrolled.

DM-FUN2-Q25NATmedium

How many integers n with 1 ≤ n ≤ 200 satisfy ⌊√n⌋ = 11?(Enter an integer.)

Answer: 23

Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. ⌊√n⌋ = k exactly when k² ≤ n < (k + 1)², so the value k is attained on a block of 2k + 1 consecutive integers.

Step by step.

  1. ⌊√n⌋ = 11 ⟺ 11² ≤ n < 12².
  2. That is 121 ≤ n ≤ 143.
  3. The count is 143 − 121 + 1 = 23.
  4. All of these lie inside 1 ≤ n ≤ 200, so nothing is excluded.

Answer: 23

Common misconception. Computing 144 − 121 = 23 and then doubting it, or writing 22 by forgetting the inclusive left endpoint. The block is 121 … 143, which is 23 integers.

Unit 6 — Mathematical Induction & Recursion 50 solved questions
Weak & strong induction 14
DM-IR6-Q01MCQeasy

For every integer n ≥ 1, the sum ∑_{i=1}^{n} i·2ⁱ is given by which one of the following closed forms?

  1. (n − 1)2ⁿ⁺¹ + 2
  2. (n + 1)2ⁿ⁺¹ − 2
  3. n·2ⁿ⁺¹ − 2ⁿ
  4. (n − 1)2ⁿ + 2
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. A sum of the form ∑ i·2ⁱ is proved by ordinary induction: assume the closed form for n = k, then add the single new term (k+1)2^{k+1} and simplify back into the same shape with k replaced by k+1. The first term gives the base case.

Step by step.

  1. Base case n = 1: the sum is 1·2 = 2. Option (A) gives (0)·4 + 2 = 2, option (B) gives 2·4 − 2 = 6, option (C) gives 1·4 − 2 = 2, option (D) gives 0 + 2 = 2. So (B) is already out, and three options survive n = 1.
  2. Second value n = 2: the sum is 2 + 8 = 10. (A) gives (1)·8 + 2 = 10; (C) gives 2·8 − 4 = 12; (D) gives 1·4 + 2 = 6. Only (A) survives.
  3. Inductive step (confirmation): assume ∑_{i=1}^{k} i·2ⁱ = (k−1)2^{k+1} + 2. Then ∑_{i=1}^{k+1} = (k−1)2^{k+1} + 2 + (k+1)2^{k+1} = 2k·2^{k+1} + 2 = k·2^{k+2} + 2, which is the same formula with k replaced by k+1.

Answer: Option (A) — (n − 1)2ⁿ⁺¹ + 2.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) gives 6 at n = 1, not 2.
  • (C) agrees at n = 1 but gives 12 at n = 2, not 10.
  • (D) agrees at n = 1 but gives 6 at n = 2, not 10.

Common misconception. Checking only n = 1 accepts three of the four options, because several formulas agree on the first value. Two test values (or a genuine induction step) are needed; this is exactly why a base case alone never proves a closed form.

Faster method. Compute the sum at n = 1 and n = 2 — the pair (2, 10) — and eliminate. Only (A) matches both.

Takeaway. For a claimed closed form, evaluate at two small values first and only then write the induction step.

DM-IR6-Q02MCQeasy

For each integer n ≥ 1 let P(n) be the statement 2ⁿ > n². A student takes n = 1 as the only base case and claims that P(k) ⇒ P(k+1) holds for every k ≥ 1. The smallest value of k for which that implication is false is

  1. 1
  2. 2
  3. 3
  4. 4
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. An induction step is an implication P(k) ⇒ P(k+1) that must be true for every k in the range. It can fail either because P(k+1) is false while P(k) is true — that is a failure of the step itself, and no amount of base-case work can repair it.

Step by step.

  1. P(1): 2¹ = 2 > 1 = 1², so P(1) is true.
  2. P(2): 2² = 4 > 4 = 2² is false. Therefore P(1) ⇒ P(2) is a true antecedent with a false consequent, so the implication fails at k = 1.
  3. P(3): 8 > 9 is also false, so the step fails at k = 2 as well; the first failure is nevertheless at k = 1.
  4. The claim itself is false for n = 2 and n = 3 and true for n = 1 and for all n ≥ 5, so this statement cannot be proved by induction starting at n = 1 at all.

Answer: Option (A) — k = 1.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) k = 2 is a second failure, not the smallest one.
  • (C) and (D): at k = 3 and k = 4 the implication is true (P(3) is false, which makes the implication vacuously true, and P(4) ⇒ P(5) is 16 > 16 false ⇒ 32 > 25 true, again vacuously true).

Common misconception. Students check the step at a large k, where it works, and conclude the proof is fine. The step must be checked for every k in the range, including the smallest one — and when the step fails, changing the base case cannot help.

Faster method. Evaluate P(1) and P(2). The very first implication is already false, so the answer is k = 1.

Takeaway. The base case and the step are separate obligations: here the base case holds and the step fails immediately.

DM-IR6-Q03NATeasy

Using the identity ∑_{i=1}^{n} i³ = (n(n+1)/2)², the value of ∑_{i=1}^{10} i³ is ______.
(Enter an integer.)

Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. The identity is the induction-friendly form of the sum of cubes: the closed form is the square of the sum of the first n integers. Once the closed form is known, the numeric answer is one substitution.

Step by step.

  1. Sum of the first 10 integers: 1 + 2 + … + 10 = 10·11/2 = 55.
  2. Square it: 55² = 3025.
  3. Cross-check with the cube values: 1 + 8 + 27 + 64 + 125 + 216 + 343 + 512 + 729 + 1000 = 3025.

Answer: 3025.

Common misconception. Forgetting the division by 2 and computing 110² = 12100, or squaring only the last term. The base of the square is the whole sum n(n+1)/2.

Faster method. 55² = 3025 — the whole question is one arithmetic step once the identity is recognised.

Takeaway. ∑ i³ = (∑ i)²; the closed form is a square, so the answer is a perfect square.

DM-IR6-Q04MCQmedium

Which one of the following statements about strong (complete) induction and ordinary (weak) induction on ℕ is TRUE?

  1. Strong induction can prove statements that ordinary induction cannot, because it assumes more.
  2. Every statement provable by strong induction is also provable by ordinary induction.
  3. A strong-induction proof needs no base case, because the hypothesis already covers the earlier values.
  4. A strong-induction proof must verify at least two base cases before the step can be applied.
Show answer & solution

Detailed solution

Concept. Strong induction assumes P(0), P(1), …, P(k) and concludes P(k+1); ordinary induction assumes only P(k). The two principles prove exactly the same set of statements, because ordinary induction applied to the auxiliary claim Q(n) = “P(j) holds for all j ≤ n” reproduces the strong step.

Step by step.

  1. Assume every statement provable by strong induction is provable by weak induction is what has to be shown. Let P be provable by strong induction. Define Q(n) as “P(0) ∧ P(1) ∧ … ∧ P(n)”.
  2. The strong step gives P(0) ∧ … ∧ P(k) ⇒ P(k+1), which is exactly Q(k) ⇒ Q(k+1). The base case P(0) gives Q(0).
  3. Ordinary induction on Q therefore gives Q(n) for all n, hence P(n) for all n. So strong induction adds no theorems.
  4. The converse is immediate: a weak step is a special case of the strong step.

Answer: Option (B) — the two principles are equivalent in strength.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) fails: the extra hypothesis is not an extra assumption, it is derived from the same data, so nothing new becomes provable.
  • (C) fails: at k = 0 the strong hypothesis is empty, so P(0) has to be proved separately.
  • (D) fails: the number of base cases depends on how far back the step reaches, not on how strong the hypothesis is.

Common misconception. “Stronger hypothesis, so stronger method.” The hypothesis is not free — it must be justified by the same induction — so the two methods are equivalent, and strong induction is simply more convenient when a step needs several earlier values.

Faster method. Strong induction = ordinary induction applied to the running conjunction Q(n). That single rewriting settles the equivalence.

Takeaway. Strong and weak induction are the same principle in different clothes; strong induction is a convenience, not an extra power.

DM-IR6-Q05MSQmedium

Which of the following statements about induction on ℕ are TRUE?

  1. In a strong-induction proof, replacing the hypothesis “P(j) holds for every j ≤ k” by “P(k) holds” may leave the proof invalid.
  2. Every proof by ordinary induction can be re-cast as a proof by strong induction with the same base cases.
